nameStory: The marbled orbweaver gets its name from the beautiful marbled patterns that swirl across its rounded abdomen, like colors mixed in stone or cake batter. Some people also call it the pumpkin spider because the female's plump, orange-tinted belly can look remarkably like a tiny Halloween pumpkin hanging in her web!
description: The marbled orbweaver is a chunky, medium-sized spider that builds classic circular webs between shrubs and low vegetation. Females have distinctively swollen, balloon-like abdomens decorated with swirling patterns in shades of orange, yellow, white, and brown. Males are much smaller and less colorful. This is one of our most variably colored orbweavers, with some individuals bright orange and others more subdued yellow or cream.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Females have remarkably inflated, almost spherical abdomens that feel firm when gently touched, like a small marble or bead

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Swirling marbled patterns in orange, yellow, white, and brown create a mottled appearance that varies dramatically between individuals

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Classic spiral orb web, usually positioned horizontally or at a slight angle, with sticky capture threads that feel tacky to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females are noticeably chunky with their swollen abdomens, while males are much smaller and slender with longer legs proportionally

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in center of web during day, and when disturbed, the web vibrates with a distinctive bouncy quality due to the spider's weight

habitat: Found in gardens, woodland edges, and shrubby areas throughout New England, particularly favoring spots with dense vegetation about 3-6 feet high. They love building webs between bushes, tall perennials, and the lower branches of small trees where there's good airflow but protection from wind. You'll often spot them in overgrown gardens, forest clearings, and along hiking trails where shrubs create natural web anchor points.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders emerge and begin building small webs. Look for tiny versions with the characteristic inflated abdomen shape, though colors may be less pronounced.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season when adults create their largest, most impressive orb webs. Females develop their most dramatic pumpkin-like abdomens and vibrant marbled coloration.
seasonality.fall: Mating season brings males searching for females in their webs. Females create egg sacs and their abdomens may appear even more swollen. Webs often collect dew beautifully on cool mornings.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off after first frost. Eggs overwinter in protected locations, often in bark crevices or under eaves where the silken egg sacs weather the cold months.

funFact: The female's inflated abdomen isn't just for show—it can actually change size throughout the day as she processes prey, sometimes deflating noticeably after she hasn't eaten for a while, then puffing back up after a big meal!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other round-bellied orbweavers, but the marbled orbweaver's distinctly swollen, almost spherical abdomen sets it apart from the more egg-shaped Cross Orbweaver or flatter Shamrock Orbweaver. Memory trick: if it looks like it swallowed a marble, it's probably the marbled orbweaver!
contextualKnowledge: The 'pumpkin spider' nickname can cause confusion since there are other orange spiders, but this specifically refers to the rounded shape rather than just the color. The scientific name 'marmoreus' literally means 'marbled' in Latin, referring to the swirled color patterns.
compareHints: Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings. While the Barn Orbweaver can also be chunky, it lacks the distinctive marbled color patterns and tends to be more uniformly colored.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
